title: SQLite
text:
Driver choice

 

 driver  accepts node, better-sqlite3 or auto. With no filename the connection is in memory. The native driver requires a Node runtime supporting node:sqlite; opening/permission errors are surfaced rather than disguised as a fallback. Install the optional better-sqlite3 peer only if selecting that driver.

   Supported operations

Prepared statements support SELECT, writes and supported RETURNING statements. The framework truncate operation becomes DELETE FROM. SQLite does not support CREATE DATABASE, DROP DATABASE or USE; those operations reject.

   Native transactions

Use  getNativeConnection()  for advanced SQLite APIs. With synchronous drivers, do not put an await between BEGIN and COMMIT: unrelated work can interleave on a shared connection. An array of JSON operations is not a transaction.

   Backup and restoration

 createSqliteConsistentBackup(native, absoluteDestination)  uses the Node live-backup interface, checks integrity and refuses an existing destination. Stop writers before restoration and test the verified copy at a new location. Do not copy an active WAL database as though the main file were a complete snapshot. Protect backup files and keep copies outside the serving host.

   Ownership

Injected databaseInstance values are not closed by the adapter. Connector-created databases close on disconnect. A local SQLite file is not a distributed database for independent filesystem hosts.
description: Choose a native SQLite driver, understand synchronous transactions and take safe backups.

title: MongoDB
text:
Connect through the manager

 

The optional Mongo driver is loaded for URI-based connections. Injected db/client/executor objects support host-managed infrastructure. URI-created clients are owned by the manager; injected clients are not disconnected automatically.

   Operation boundary

The adapter translates normalized operations into Mongo operators and aggregation pipelines. Joins, groups and unions need schema-specific verification; this is not a complete SQL engine. Unsupported alterations and selector operators reject explicitly.

   Writes and authorization

Unsafe field/document keys are rejected. Unfiltered update/delete fails closed unless explicitly enabled. Still enforce tenant and operation authorization in application code: preventing unsafe syntax does not decide which user may modify a document.

   Transactions and production

Use real Mongo sessions/transactions for atomic multi-document work and journals. Configure authentication, TLS, selection timeouts, retries and indexes for your deployment. An operation array is not automatically a transaction, and SQLite tests do not certify Mongo concurrency behavior.

title: Shared SQL compiler
text:
Intended audience

Applications should use @zeruxjs/db with a concrete connector. This package is primarily for connector implementers who need parameterized SQL generation and normalized execution results.

   Compilation contract

 createSqlConnector(dialect, options)  translates a normalized operation through a dialect. Values become parameters. Identifiers and runtime operator/function/join/order enums are validated and quoted. Arbitrary textual CHECK expressions are rejected in favor of a structured expression.

   Result contract

Write results preserve affected counts; a zero-row update is important for compare-and-swap. Insert IDs are emitted for actual inserts, not DDL or updates. SQLite bigint IDs may be normalized to strings to preserve precision. Dialects have distinct index, autoincrement and RETURNING support.

   Trust and transaction boundary

Parameterized values do not authorize a schema operation. Keep credentials narrow and never expose unrestricted SQL compilation to clients. Each operation executes independently unless a native transaction context is explicitly provided. Adapter changes require verification against each supported real database engine.

title: Server hooks and request scope
text:
Request isolation

The hooks package uses AsyncLocalStorage for scoped server state. Enter  runWithRequestHooks  for a request and execute synchronous render functions through  runHooks .

 

   Render rules

Call hooks in a stable order and count. The package detects mismatched hook sequences. Hook rendering is synchronous; setting state does not schedule a React/Zyro rerender. The application owns rerender scheduling. Effects clean up on dependency changes and disposal.

   Context

Use createContext, setContext and useContext for request-local values.  withContext  supports nested overrides. Do not replace request-scoped state with module-level variables for identity, locale or tenant selection.

   Path registries

 createPathRegistry({ directory })  stores aliases with validated names and atomic private writes. Legacy wrappers select the working directory at invocation time. Atomic replacement avoids partial files but not lost updates across processes; serialize writers or use a database.

   Cleanup

Dispose component hooks when the render owner no longer needs them. Explicit cleanup matters for effects and retained resources. This package is not React Hooks and does not install a UI renderer.

title: Authentication and authorization
text:
Choose a complete flow

The package supplies primitives: password hashing/verification, encrypted sessions, user/role database helpers, OTPs, TOTP, scoped tokens and PKCE preparation. Your application still owns login routes, cookies, CSRF, rate limits, user recovery and authorization decisions.

   TOTP and scoped tokens

 

Encrypt enrollment secrets at rest and do not log the URI or tokens. TOTP verification alone does not stop replay; record accepted time steps. OTP hashes need persisted expiry, attempt limits and one-time consumption.

   Sessions and revocation

Securely configure SECURITY_SESSION_KEY, SECURITY_SESSION_SALT and SECURITY_PASSWORD_SALT. Rotation needs a migration plan. Built-in token/revocation stores are in-memory; use shared persistent state for multiple servers, restart survival and global revocation. Set safe cookie attributes and protect unsafe cookie-authenticated requests against CSRF.

   Tenant permissions

 hasTenantPermission  /  requireTenantPermission  demand an authenticated principal, exact tenant and explicit permission, with optional site scope. There is no implicit wildcard administrator. Construct that principal from verified identity and server-side membership, never a submitted role object.

   OAuth and passkeys

PKCE helpers prepare state/verifier and the authorization URL. Store them per login attempt and validate state before exchanging a code. They do not exchange tokens or verify provider ID tokens. Passkey challenge generation is not WebAuthn attestation/assertion verification; use a complete verifier for passkey authentication.

title: Security primitives
text:
Compose policies

 

The request, sessionId and response integration are application-provided. Supply a sufficiently strong server-held CSRF secret. A helper returns a policy result; ensure the actual response/handler enforces it.

   CORS versus authorization

An origin allowlist controls browser cross-origin access. It does not authenticate a caller, prevent server-to-server requests or prove tenant membership. Authorize the operation independently. For cookie-authenticated writes, verify origin where supplied and a session-bound CSRF token.

   Rate limiting

 createRateLimiter  is in-memory. Multiple replicas do not share its counters. Configure limits at the edge or use an appropriate shared backend when a global limit matters. Choose identity keys from trusted context rather than arbitrary forwarded headers.

   Filesystem and headers

 ensurePathInsideRoot  is lexical containment, not symlink-safe filesystem authorization. Use appropriate secure file-descriptor handling for private data. A default security-header set is not an XSS proof; configure CSP for your application's assets and avoid unsafe HTML interpolation.

title: Object and file storage
text:
Manager and addresses

An object address is  { storage, bucket, key } . The manager selects a named driver and enforces configured bucket/type/size rules. Store private files outside public web roots.

 

   Read, copy and serve

Use stat/read for trusted server access.  createFileResponse  integrates Fetch streaming, conditional requests and supported ranges. Private responses require authorization; uploads need explicit write permission and a byte limit. The publicUrl formatter does not grant access or configure a bucket ACL.

   S3-compatible providers

createS3Storage supports AWS and compatible endpoints with region, endpoint and path-style options. Choose one credential mode: default chain, profile, explicit credentials, assume-role or web identity. Provider capabilities differ for multipart, KMS, ACLs and signing; verify the real provider rather than assuming universal parity.

   Integrity and limits

Manager copies enforce destination type and maximum bytes, including native storage copies. Encrypted local objects verify authentication before plaintext output and do not support byte ranges. A signed upload URL is a capability, not proof that its recipient is authorized for another tenant's key.

   Lifecycle

Framework configuration can own the manager; otherwise call close during shutdown. Use filesystem/provider permissions, lifecycle/retention policies and a malware/content policy appropriate to uploads. Local S3-lite is an object-addressing interface, not a complete S3 HTTP server.

title: Private media
text:
Storage choices

The legacy local media store uses random IDs, disk files and metadata. For multi-host storage use the files-backed integration and a shared authorized backend. Neither option supplies application login or tenant permission automatically.

 

   Upload contract

The helper streams raw request bytes; it does not parse multipart/form-data. It checks maximum bytes and declared length. The application owns MIME validation, compression policy, malware scanning, quotas and permission to create the destination object.

   Downloads and integrity

HTTP helpers support HEAD, ETags, conditional requests and single/suffix ranges, with private no-store defaults. Full download verifies SHA-256; streamed partial reads verify size but do not compute a complete digest before emitting data. Restrict inline rendering to trusted inert types.

   Capabilities and listing

Signed media tokens are short-lived capabilities with an application signing key, not user authentication. For client-facing files-backed metadata use statAuthorized/listAuthorized. Partition tenant listings by bucket/key prefix when complete authorized pagination matters. Schedule expiration cleanup and keep storage outside public directories.

title: Search indexes
text:
Build an index

 

The index supports relevance scoring, field weighting, replacements/removals, filters, pagination, suggestions and snapshots. Values are defensively copied. It is an in-memory index, not a synchronized search cluster.

   HTTP helper

Import createSearchHandler from @zeruxjs/search/http and register it with the Fetch bridge. It handles bounded GET/HEAD queries, projection, suggestions, cache validators and pagination. Without projection, full matching documents can be returned: index only public fields for a public endpoint.

   Private search

Never use a shared response cache when applying user/tenant visibility filters. Authenticated requests use no-store; filtered indexes disable suggestions to avoid leaking vocabulary. Apply authorization before indexing or returning protected material.

   Persistence

The Node-only persistence export saves/loads snapshots with atomic replacement and symlink checks. The parent directory must already exist. A single-writer local snapshot is not distributed coordination or an authoritative database. Rebuild from source data when the index format/content changes.

title: Analytics collection and aggregates
text:
Create an event pipeline

 

The database manager is application-provided and must have the named connection. Collection is best effort: unavailable storage, validation or writes can drop events without failing the user request. A 204 collector response is not proof of a committed event.

   Public collection policy

Use explicit origins, bounded body readers, timeouts and concurrency. Browser consent/identity must be configured intentionally; the library does not create tracking cookies or fingerprint users automatically. Bind site by trusted origin for multi-tenant collection and authenticate confidential server events.

   Query coverage

  Query   Meaning  
  ---   ---  
  Bounded raw events   A limited event page, not a global total  
  Native aggregate/count   Exact for persisted matching event rows  
  Numeric materialization   Indexed-only facts; historical/failed writes can be missing  
  Reconciliation completion   A bounded scan exhausted, not a transactional completeness proof  

   Request IDs and control-plane storage

Use the shared database request-ID store for cross-replica day-scoped replay protection. Memory reservations only coordinate one process. Versioned document stores require atomic affected-count CAS semantics. They are not high-volume durable ingestion queues.

   Email activity and retention

Email instrumentation is separately opt-in and can use a rotating key ring. Opens are observed requests that can include scanners/proxies. A clicked download link does not prove bytes were served. Retention APIs are paged and require explicit approval; they do not erase every external or email-related record. Review the full package documentation before enabling deletion or interpreting totals.
description: Collect opt-in events and interpret each query’s coverage honestly.

title: Email delivery, inboxes and campaigns
text:
Configure an SMTP manager

 

   Consent is not tracking

Marketing sends require an affirmative current subscription from an injected preferences service. Transactional purpose is separate. Neither permission nor an unsubscribe silently changes message tracking. Instrumentation is per-send opt-in and explicit send options can disable it.

   Templates and attachments

Use escaped template variables and the email layout helpers for supported email-safe markup. Converting arbitrary browser HTML/CSS cannot make every mail client support it. Attachments can stream from the files manager with configured bounds; do not accept arbitrary local paths from clients.

   Queues and delivery ambiguity

The built-in transient queue and manager-lifetime idempotency are not durable exactly-once delivery. Use persisted message IDs with the BullMQ adapters and a shared CAS delivery record for restart-safe workflows. SMTP timeout after acceptance can be ambiguous; mark uncertain outcomes for operator reconciliation rather than blindly resending.

   Inbound mail

createEmailReceiver supports configured IMAP/POP3 polling, MIME parsing and attachment policies. Choose package-managed/mapped/custom inbox storage or JSON-only mode. Persist cursors per mailbox and verify access for UI APIs. POP3 cannot mutate IMAP-style flags; JSON-only receive mode does not deduplicate for you.

   Campaigns and governance

Campaign planning, outbox checkpoints, suppression, dashboards and exports are opt-in application integrations. Supply host authorization, consent checks, durable stores and signed provider webhook verification. Archive is not deletion; redaction has retention/legal-hold boundaries. The package README includes the detailed contracts for each subsystem.
description: Separate transport, consent, tracking, scheduling and durable delivery state.

title: Queues and background jobs
text:
Producer and worker roles

A queue service manages named BullMQ queues. Producers add small job payloads; designated worker processes execute processors. Do not register processors on every web replica unless that deployment is intentional.

 

   Retry policy

BullMQ jobs are at-least-once. Make handlers idempotent through authoritative storage, not only a job ID. Producers fail quickly during Redis outages; worker connections use the blocking-operation retry policy. Delay/repeat schedules need live workers and durable Redis persistence.

   Data and lifecycle

Store identifiers rather than bodies, recipients, credentials or personal data in Redis. Queue cleanup precedes cache/database cleanup. Keep BullMQ prefix separate from cache prefixes and never use ioredis keyPrefix. Use noeviction and a persistence policy appropriate to recovery needs.

   Administration

Operations are denied without administration.authorize. The optional dashboard additionally requires host session authentication and CSRF callbacks. Inspect returns bounded redacted summaries; raw queue job APIs can reveal private data and are trusted server-only. Queue pause is global; worker pause affects one process.

   Durable email and events

The durable email processor uses a host-supplied atomic CAS record and treats sending failures/expired sending leases as uncertain. QueueEvents is a bounded stream, not a permanent audit trail. Persist operational events separately when retention matters and reconcile uncertain sends with provider evidence.
description: Use durable Redis scheduling with explicit workers and at-least-once handling.

title: Browser and server tagging
text:
The service boundary

Tags connect browser ttag, request-scoped server astag, trigger definitions and approved destinations. The default internal analytics tag records matching events; GA4 Measurement Protocol and approved HTTPS webhooks execute server-side so destination credentials do not enter public container JSON.

   Browser collection

Load the configured /_tags/ttag.js route after establishing an intentional consent policy. Use ttag event/set/get/consent operations. Denied consent discards queued events. Browser events are delivered asynchronously and best effort; a generated request ID does not prove delivery or legal consent.

   Server context

Create astag for a request with a trusted site and approved identity context. Do not share one mutable astag singleton across users. Use a shared database request-ID store for cross-replica uniqueness and siteByOrigin for public tenant binding.

   Studio and releases

Admin routes require host authorization; writes need same-origin checks and optimistic versions. Publish/preview controls and bounded release snapshots do not replace transactional control-plane storage at large scale. No arbitrary browser JavaScript/HTML tags are executed.

   Egress

Destination timeouts isolate failures, but HTTPS hostname validation alone does not remove DNS rebinding risk. Deploy outbound DNS/IP allowlists and firewall rules. Google HTTP acceptance is not proof of GA4 processing. Email marketing consent is independent of telemetry consent.

title: Reports and dashboards
text:
Source and authorization

Reports query internal analytics, not arbitrary SQL or executable chart code. A host authorize callback is required; missing authorization disables the service. Grant read, edit, export, sensitive-property and campaign access independently where needed.

   Definition ownership

Reports contain pages and charts. Definition updates use same-origin JSON writes and optimistic CAS. For multi-tenant hosts, resolve a trusted tenant scope with a dedicated document store, not merely a site filter over one global document. Never accept tenant scope from an unverified query parameter.

   Query modes

Native count dimensions can query all persisted matching rows. Supported numeric fields use indexed-only materialized facts. Other queries can fall back to a bounded sample (commonly 500 raw rows). Display queryMode, truncation and coverage in every dashboard/export; sampled totals cannot be represented as all-time facts.

   Exports and campaigns

CSV/JSON exports require separate permission and have byte/chart/query-budget caps. They are individual chart queries, not a transactional historical snapshot. Campaign views distinguish SMTP acceptance, provider notifications and observed tracking events; those are different measurements.

   Operations

Use secure host sessions, tenant filters and trusted source adapters. Dashboards do not ship an identity provider or default password. Large reports need warehouse/native aggregation capabilities and independent rate limits; the studio is not a general BI connector platform.

title: AI chat providers
text:
Construct the provider

 

This is an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions transport, not a complete provider SDK or Responses API adapter. Credentials stay on the server. HTTPS or loopback HTTP endpoints are accepted; redirects are rejected to avoid forwarding bearer credentials elsewhere.

   Streaming

SSE text is decoded across network and UTF-8 boundaries with total/frame size bounds. Streams emit text only, not complete tool/multimodal event structures. Stop iteration or abort to cancel and release concurrency slots.

   Retry and fallback

withRetry retries explicit retryable provider failures with bounded delay; arbitrary errors are not automatically retried. It does not replay an already-started stream. Fallback can select another provider only before output has been emitted, and aborts must remain aborts.

   Application responsibilities

Authorize requests, cap input/output budgets, manage cost and redact sensitive prompts/logs. Provider output is untrusted text, not executable HTML or a policy decision. Validate any tool action in trusted application code.

title: Retrieval knowledge bases
text:
What the package does

This is a local keyword retrieval/chunking layer, not model training, embeddings or a vector database. It ranks source documents, budgets excerpts and can pass evidence to a compatible chat provider.

 

   Identity and persistence

Chunk IDs are deterministic and carry source metadata. Snapshot imports reject duplicate IDs and use bounded atomic filesystem writes with symlink checks. Serialize writers; local snapshots do not coordinate separate machines.

   Grounded answers

text:
Independent runners

 

The runners return error/warning results. Make the process exit nonzero on failed checks; do not print and discard the result. lintAll composes checks and runPrettier handles formatting.

   Boundaries

Discovery skips generated directories, symlinks and oversized files with file-count bounds. Read-only mode does not apply fixes. Formatting differences count as failures without fix. Project config/plugins are executable trusted code, not safe inputs from untrusted requests.

title: Contributing to the docs
text:
Content format

Each version has a flat directory of Markdown files in apps/zerux-docs/src/docs/<version /. A file starts with a JSON metadata block delimited by --- lines, followed by ordinary Markdown. JSON makes metadata validation explicit and avoids ambiguous YAML coercions.

 

The filename determines the stable slug. Include package for a package guide, for example @zeruxjs/cache. Exactly one authored guide may claim a package for a version.

   Author useful pages

Explain when to use a feature, show a minimal complete example, define ownership and cleanup, cover errors/constraints, and link the implementation. Use real public imports. Distinguish standalone package configuration from framework startup configuration. Define application-supplied callbacks instead of presenting them as built-ins.

   Markdown conventions

Use level-two headings for primary sections and level-three for subsections. Stable unique heading slugs become table-of-contents links. Link to another page as [label](routing.md), including a heading fragment if necessary. Fenced code accepts a language and an optional title attribute for a filename. Tables, lists, blockquotes and inline code use standard Markdown. Raw HTML is escaped; do not embed script tags or executable MDX.

   Build validation

Run npm run build in apps/zerux-docs. The build rejects missing metadata, unknown sections, broken source references, duplicate routes/IDs, invalid related pages, missing static assets and broken local links/anchors. It checks search entries too, and promotes the new output only after validation. npm run check rechecks an existing export.

   Add a documentation version

Before bumping live packages, run npm run snapshot -- <old-version . Commit the reference.snapshot.json file, mark that version reference as snapshot in src/site.config.mjs, and pin its ref to a Git commit/tag. Add the new version and copy/review its Markdown directory, then set site.latest. Version switching keeps the current slug when it exists or falls back to introduction.

Do not leave old documentation reading current manifests: that silently changes archived API contracts. The live reference builder requires the framework version to match the live docs version; independently released ecosystem packages keep their own versions.

   Review expectations

Keep reference links and examples synchronized with code. State implementation boundaries without claiming a whole framework ecosystem from a package name. Security, durability, authorization and query coverage should be described at the relevant API boundary, not only in a generic disclaimer. Review both desktop and mobile output and exercise keyboard navigation when changing presentation.
description: Author, validate, version and extend the documentation without editing the renderer.

text:
ZCLIVO — composable CLI toolkit

Command registry and explicit plugin discovery for ZeruxJS, ZyroJS, and other JavaScript applications.   This is an evolving 0.x package.   Commands can be shared under a common keyword without requiring plugins to mutate a global command map or immediately call  process.exit() .

   Programmatic command registry

 

Supports named/positional arguments, repeated flags, aliases,  --help ,  --docs ,  --completion , strict typed flags, required/default/choice validation, and reusable command definitions. No handlers are executed during registration.

   Shared commands from multiple packages

  Only explicitly configured plugins are loaded.   Declare allowlisted plugins in the application's  package.json :

 

Each installed plugin has a  zerux  entry in its own manifest:

 

Its entry exports a  register  function:

 

Load via  await loadConfiguredPlugins(registry, projectRoot)  or  await loadPlugins(['my-zerux-plugin'], registry, projectRoot) .

Plugins are   trusted executable code  , not sandboxed extensions. Entry paths are checked using canonical filesystem paths and cannot escape their owning package through symlinks or traversal. Plugins are no longer automatically loaded from every installed  node_modules  package.

   Existing ZeruxJS compatibility

 import { cli } from 'zclivo'  still exposes  cli.addKey(keyword, {func,description})  and  cli.addCommand(keyword, name, handler, options)  with the same parsed argument structure. Legacy handlers no longer cause an immediate  process.exit() ; set  process.exitCode  if an explicit exit status is needed. Asynchronous development servers continue to run while they have active handles.

   Validation

 

   Section 79 — safe app starter

After installing/building this package, use  zclivo create my-app  (TypeScript),
 zclivo create my-app --js  (JavaScript), or  zclivo create my-app --dry-run  to inspect
what will be written. Programmatic usage:

 

The destination must be a new, non-hidden directory with an existing parent.
The generator stages files, claims its target directory exclusively, refuses
existing files/directories   including dangling symlinks  , and cleans up on
failed writes; no  --force  overwrite or shell command is run. Starters use only
public  zeruxjs  dependencies and Node's test runner. The generated source is
intentionally minimal—not a fully integrated demo or live-deployment proof.
 npm install ,  npm run dev ,  npm run build , browser acceptance and real service
configuration must be verified separately in a clean environment.

title: Proxy request hardening (Section 7)
text:
The portless proxy now validates Host / HTTP/2 authority before routing, handles IPv6 authorities, and prefers the longest matching registered suffix. Untrusted  Forwarded  and  X-Forwarded-   input is discarded; the proxy reconstructs forwarding headers from the socket and requested authority. Malformed hop counts are rejected, and upstream HTTP and WebSocket handshake requests have a 30-second socket timeout. 

 Run focused regression tests after building:  node --test test/request-security.test.mjs . This local development proxy is   not   a substitute for an authenticated public reverse proxy.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Proxy lifecycle and WebSocket behavior
text:
The portless proxy supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 over TLS, and HTTP/1.1 WebSocket upgrades. Upgrade handshake bytes are forwarded only after the upstream returns  101 Switching Protocols ; both tunnel sockets are cleaned up on disconnect. A 30-second upstream handshake timeout applies before an upgrade, while an established WebSocket tunnel is not subject to this handshake timeout. 

  portlessStop()  rejects malformed PID files and refuses to signal a process unless the expected proxy is responding. If the PID no longer exists, it removes the stale marker.   Note:   an HTTP health check does not establish cryptographic process identity; do not share the proxy state directory with untrusted users. The proxy remains intended for local development. A graceful-drain shutdown, stronger process ownership verification, and production hardening remain future work. 

 Focused regression tests are in  test/websocket-proxy.test.mjs  and  test/lifecycle.test.mjs .
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Atomic proxy state and recovery (Section 16)
text:
zhost  now writes  proxy.state.json  as the   last, atomic commit record  
containing the port, TLS flag, TLD and verified process marker. The existing
 proxy.port ,  proxy.tls ,  proxy.tld  and  proxy.pid  files remain for older
consumers. Internal discovery reads the committed record as one snapshot instead
of combining independently updated files. 

 A  .proxy-startup-journal.json  left behind by an interrupted publication
causes state readers to fail closed with  PendingStartupTransactionError .
The next coordinated startup recovers the journal under its directory lock,
subject to conflict and live-owner checks. Manual consumers can call
 recoverInterruptedStartup(stateDir)    only while holding  
 withOperationLock(stateDir, ...) . 

 Legacy installations without  proxy.state.json  are read using a verified
double snapshot until their next successful startup. Legacy reads cannot offer
the same atomic guarantee as a commit record; do not edit state files manually.
A malformed commit record or unresolved journal is not silently ignored.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Safe route lifecycle and registry protection (Section 17)
text:
Applications launched with  portlessRun()  now receive a unique route lease.
When the child command finishes, its cleanup only removes   that registration  ;
if another app has replaced the hostname (including  --force  takeover), the
older app cannot delete the replacement. Explicit administrative  removeRoute() 
remains unconditional, and the original  addRoute()  API retains the legacy
on-disk route format. 

 For integrations that manage application processes themselves: 

 

 The route registry rejects malformed, duplicated, oversized, or symlinked
 routes.json  files when making changes rather than silently overwriting them.
Reader APIs remain lenient for UI display. The route mutation lock stores an
OS-specific process identity: it will not steal a slow, active owner's lock
based on file age alone. Verified dead owners can be recovered. An ownerless,
malformed, or unverifiable lock requires manual inspection. 

 To run the route-focused regression tests after compiling the package:
 node --test test/routes.test.mjs test/route-leases.test.mjs . 

   Deployment note:   This continues to be a local-development proxy. Route
leases prevent accidental cleanup races; they do not provide user isolation,
authenticated registration, or a hardened internet-facing control plane.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Application supervision and readiness (Section 18)
text:
zerux-server run  now launches application commands   without shell interpolation  ,
checks for an already occupied application port, waits for a TCP listener on
 127.0.0.1 , and   only then   publishes the hostname route. If the process
crashes, fails to spawn, or misses its readiness deadline, no route is published
and the child is stopped/reaped. The parent forwards SIGINT/SIGTERM, sends them
to the entire spawned POSIX process group, waits up to a bounded timeout, and
uses SIGKILL if necessary. Route cleanup remains ownership-aware. 

 

 All   launcher flags precede the application command   (optionally separated by
 -- ). Anything after the command is passed to the child verbatim, including
 --port ,  --name  and  -- . Use  --no-ready  only for long-running processes
without a TCP readiness endpoint; in this mode a route can be published before
the app is actually ready. When supplying  --app-port , the port must be free. 

 For library integrations,  launchSupervisedCommand(argv, { port, onExit }) 
returns a  SupervisedProcess  with  .completed ,  .running , and asynchronous
 .stop() .  spawnCommand  is retained as a compatibility wrapper, but new code
should use the supervisor API. On Windows, direct execution does not invoke a
shell; prefer executable programs or invoke scripts through  node  explicitly. 

   Section 18 limitations:   Basic TCP readiness confirms a listener, not an HTTP health endpoint;
free-port discovery cannot eliminate races before the child binds. Child-process
group termination is strongest on POSIX; native Windows process-tree supervision
still needs its own integration suite. This tool is intended for local developer
applications, not untrusted multi-tenant process execution. 

 Focused checks after compilation:  node --test test/process-supervisor.test.mjs
test/cli-run-arguments.test.mjs test/app-supervision-integration.test.mjs .
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: HTTP health checks and bounded restart policies (Section 19)
text:
When an application supplies an HTTP health endpoint, ZHOST can wait for a
successful status (HTTP 200–299) before publishing a route. Health requests are
GET requests to  127.0.0.1 , do not follow redirects, have bounded timeouts,
and discard response bodies. A failing runtime health check removes the route,
stops the unhealthy child, and optionally starts a new process. 

 

  --restart  accepts  never  (default, preserves previous behavior),
 on-failure , and  always . Restarts have capped exponential delays. The
 --max-restarts  quota applies within the  --restart-window  time interval,
and failed restarts also count toward the budget. Once exhausted, the wrapper
exits with a failure.  --health-path  enables HTTP readiness and 10-second
runtime monitoring by default.  --health-interval  adjusts this cadence.
 --health-failures  is the number of consecutive failed probes before the
supervisor stops a running process. With no HTTP path, monitoring checks TCP
connectivity. A  --no-ready  application cannot enable health monitoring. 

 For library clients, use  launchManagedApplication(argv, { port, health,
restartPolicy, onReady }) .  onReady  may return a disposal function (such as
releasing a route lease). It is called after each successful readiness check;
the disposer is called on exit before any restart. The controller has
 .current ,  .running ,  .completed , and  .stop() . Additional exports include
 probeApplicationHealth()  and  validateManagedOptions() . 

   Production boundary:   Restart budgets and counters exist only in the
supervising process; restarts are sequential and not zero-downtime. HTTP probes
do not authenticate the application's content, and cannot replace production
load-balancer health checks. The supervisor is for trusted local applications,
not a privilege boundary for executing untrusted commands. Windows process tree
behavior and cross-process recovery still need native integration testing. 

 Regression suite (after building dependencies and  zhost ):
 node --test test/ .test.mjs .
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Runtime status and coordinated manual reload (Section 20)
text:
Managed application state is now observable via  handle.status  and
 handle.subscribe(listener) . Snapshots include lifecycle phase, child PID,
ready-generation number, automatic restart count, previous exit and timestamp.
Subscribe callbacks are isolated so a throwing observer cannot take down an app. 

 

 Concurrent  .restart()  calls coalesce into one request and an explicit restart
  does not use the automatic failure budget  . A stopped app refuses manual
restart. Manual restarts are sequential,   not zero-downtime  ; the route is
unpublished while its child restarts. 

 To enable a manual restart signal for a CLI-launched app on Linux/macOS: 

 

  --reload-signal  is opt-in and is not installed on Windows. Only signal a
wrapper you own; the status command   never sends signals  . Status JSON lives
under a per-user  app-status-<uid   folder inside the proxy state directory;
files are private (0600), atomically rewritten, and checked for malformed
content or symlinks. They do   not   contain CLI arguments, environment
variables, or credentials.  alive  requires verification of the wrapper's
process creation identity, not merely the PID. A  stale  result indicates
that the previous status cannot be verified as live; it is   not   a positive
application-health result. Historical terminal snapshots are retained for
troubleshooting, and may be removed manually from the private status folder. 

 This is local-machine observability, not a distributed control plane or an
authenticated remote management API. End-to-end Linux testing is included;
native macOS/Windows behavior requires additional platform verification.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Multi-instance routing and safe traffic handovers (Section 21)
text:
Route pools can distribute   new HTTP requests and WebSocket upgrades   across
up to 32 local application instances using smooth weighted round-robin. Legacy
single-port routes are unchanged. The proxy selects only loopback ports; it
never accepts remote backend addresses from route files. 

 

 -  RouteStore.registerPoolRoute()  saves validated weighted targets atomically
  and returns a lease.  lease.switchBackends()  swaps targets under the same
  route lock and fails safely if another process took over the hostname.
-  handoverBackends()  checks the  new  targets before committing; failed probes
  or invalid targets leave the currently published route unchanged.
- The proxy isolates failed upstream connections. With an active probe interval,
  isolated instances recover only after a successful check. Without an interval,
  passive failures recover after the configured cooldown. When all instances
  are unhealthy, new requests receive HTTP   503   rather than being routed to
  a known failed instance.
-  BackendPool.status()  exposes per-instance health and failure information.
  Background health probes are bounded to eight concurrent connections and
  cleaned up when the proxy listener closes.
- Manual handovers only switch   new   requests. They do not spawn new child
  servers, kill old ones, migrate existing WebSocket sessions, or guarantee
  uninterrupted availability when the old process is stopped too early. The
  deployment controller must manage the overlap and connection-drain period.
- This is still a local-development proxy. It is not an internet-facing load
  balancer, authenticated service mesh, or distributed routing coordinator. 

 After a package build, run  node --test test/backend- .test.mjs  for the new
pool, handover, and WebSocket integration regression tests.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Rolling application deployments (Section 22)
text:
launchRollingApplication  runs  overlapping  generations of the same loopback
application on different ports, tests the candidate's readiness, switches the
existing leased hostname atomically, and retires the previous child after its
in-flight proxy connections finish (or a configured drain deadline elapses).
It is an opt-in API; existing  zerux-server run  behavior is unchanged. 

 The   proxy and controller must share the same  BackendConnections  instance  .
This release does not provide cross-process drain coordination; do not use a
tracker from an unrelated proxy instance to claim uninterrupted deployments. 

 

 The child server   must bind to  127.0.0.1:${process.env.PORT}   . Ports must be
available, different, and exclusively owned by this deployment controller.
The controller passes the correct  PORT  to each child even if an existing
 env.PORT  was set. Health probes are loopback-only and do not follow redirects.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Safety and limitations
text:
-   Pre-publication failure:   failed process start, timeout, or failed initial
  health verification leaves the old route and process untouched.
-   Post-publication failure:   verification detects a failure and conditionally
  switches traffic back to the still-running old instance before stopping the
  candidate. If another process superseded the route lease, this controller
  cannot overwrite it during rollback.
-   Drain:   existing HTTP requests and upgraded WebSockets remain pinned to
  the old backend.  drained: false  means the deadline elapsed, so terminating
  the old process may interrupt remaining sessions.
-   Stop:   removes the route only if this controller still owns its lease;
  waits for current traffic and terminates the child. Repeated stops and
  concurrent deploy requests are coalesced.
- This is a   same-machine, same-process-proxy   orchestration API, not a
  distributed deployment system, persistent supervisor, or cross-process
  zero-downtime controller. It does not automatically roll back a deployment
  after the verification window has ended. 

 Focused validation: build  zhost , then run
 node --test test/rolling-app.test.mjs test/backend- .test.mjs .
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Rolling CLI & cross-process deployment control (Section 23)
text:
The Section 22 rolling controller is now available from the CLI, with   real
proxy-side HTTP/WebSocket drain observations   even when the proxy and the
application wrapper are separate processes. Use an existing ZHOST proxy built
from this version or later; rolling launches deliberately refuse to claim
traffic has drained when they cannot reach its authenticated control endpoint. 

 

  rolling run  keeps a supervising process alive. Deploy starts a replacement on
the spare port, waits for health, switches the leased route, verifies health,
then asks the actual proxy to wait for outstanding HTTP requests and WebSocket
tunnels before stopping the old process. When the drain deadline expires,
 drained: false  is recorded and the old child is stopped. Failure before
cutover leaves the old route available; failure during the verification window
attempts a lease-checked rollback. Deployment commands are serialized by the
supervisor; multiple concurrent requests share the same in-flight deployment. 

 The CLI control endpoint listens   only   on IPv4 loopback with a random
256-bit bearer token. Its discovery descriptor and bounded deployment history
live in a private, same-user directory beneath the selected proxy state
directory. Descriptors require a verified process-start fingerprint. Requests
and responses are size-limited and time-limited; arbitrary command execution,
file access and unauthenticated process signaling are not exposed through RPC.
 rolling status  displays  last known  state and separately reports whether the
owning controller is online. History keeps up to 50 events per hostname, with
no application argv or environment secrets saved. 

   Operational boundaries:   this is local, single-host orchestration for
trusted application commands, not a publicly exposed management API or a
cross-host control plane. Both proxy and rolling wrapper must be accessible to
the same OS user; a root-owned privileged proxy control is not exposed to
another user. Abrupt supervisor termination (for example  SIGKILL  or power
loss) cannot guarantee cleanup of detached application children; stale routes
are filtered by owner liveness and require inspection. Multi-file crash
consistency, distributed scheduling and external load-balancer draining are
not provided. Run  node --test test/rolling-cli-control.test.mjs  against fresh
compiled output for a separate-process smoke test.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Recovering rolling applications after a hard crash (Section 24)
text:
The rolling wrapper now records its own OS creation fingerprint and the
fingerprints/ports of   each spawned generation   in a private, atomically
replaced  app-controls-<uid / .generations.json  file. Recording happens before
readiness and the initial route lease is saved before launch returns. A normal
stop removes this recovery record only after the supervised children have
exited. A new  rolling run  automatically attempts recovery of an abandoned
record while holding the deployment operation lock. 

 

 Recovery is intentionally conservative: it will not stop a live wrapper, a
process with an unreadable creation fingerprint, or a different process that
has reused an old PID. Recorded route leases are released conditionally, so a
newer owner's route is never removed. Recovery uses process-group signals on
POSIX only when the original group leader can still be identified; if the
leader is already gone but grandchildren survive independently, operator
cleanup may still be needed. It is not a distributed process manager or an
unattended repair tool for other users' processes. 

 Deployment history now has a default 90-day retention window (in addition to
the existing 50-event maximum).  rolling prune  accepts 0–3650 days and 0–50
events, refuses to modify a live controller's history, and preserves the most
recent status. History is informational and is never a source of authority
for process termination. Cross-platform process identity behavior still needs
native Windows/macOS integration testing.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Persistent backend health and multi-app reconciliation (Section 25)
text:
ZHOST's built-in proxy now checkpoints recent backend circuit-breaker state in
 app-controls-<uid /backend-health.json  using private atomic writes. Checkpoints
are bounded, coalesced (250 ms by default), and expire after 60 seconds. Routes
carry a registration lease/process signature: a new registration, different
backend pool, or process takeover   never inherits the previous route's
isolation state  . Late upstream responses from a replaced route cannot clear
or poison the new route's health status. Active health probes can rehabilitate
isolated backends. The standalone  createProxyServer()  API can opt into
checkpoints via  backendHealth.stateDir ; normal  portlessProxy()  configures a
private directory automatically. 

 

 The proxy also serves read-only per-backend status through its authenticated
local RPC (not over public HTTP): 

 

 Orphaned rolling controllers can be scanned and reconciled in one operation.
The scan is capped at 128 private records by default; it refuses live owners,
invalid records, and processes whose identity cannot be verified. One corrupt
record does not hide the status of other applications: 

 

   Safety boundaries:   Reconciliation is an explicit operator command, not a
periodic background daemon;  rolling run  still automatically recovers its own
abandoned controller before startup. Circuit-breaker checkpoints describe
recent failures and are not durable application or process authority.
No cross-host storage, distributed failover, or persistent metrics database is
provided. State files must remain private to the proxy's operating-system user.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Health-aware multi-instance process fleets (Section 26)
text:
launchInstanceFleet()  manages a desired set of local application processes and
publishes their backend ports through a conditional route lease. It detects
crashes and health failures, isolates unhealthy instances, launches verified
replacements using a bounded restart budget, and drains retired HTTP/WebSocket
connections before terminating the old generation. This complements the
single-instance  launchRollingApplication()  API. 

 

 The fleet API is exported from the root package. Create the proxy using your
existing ZHOST proxy setup; do not create a separate empty tracker for draining.
 fleet.stop()  is required during application shutdown. Restart budgets are
currently in memory and the API does not perform cross-process ownership
recovery automatically. See  SECTION_26_MULTI_INSTANCE_SUPERVISION.md  in the
project root for operational details and limitations.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Persistent multi-instance fleet CLI (Section 27)
text:
zerux-server fleet  connects the Section 26 multi-instance supervisor to the
real proxy's private authenticated control endpoint. Unlike launching the API
from another process, the CLI uses the proxy's   actual   connection tracker
for draining; it refuses to launch when that control is unavailable. 

 

 A strict  --  separator protects application arguments from being interpreted
as supervisor flags. The  run  command accepts 2–16 replicas and at least one
spare port. Application children bind loopback  PORT ; an optional HTTP health
path must be an origin-form relative path. A successful initial health check
is mandatory before the route is published. 

 The controller records PID + OS process-start fingerprints for every detached
generation   before readiness  , and saves its route lease before returning a
running supervisor. Live operation uses a local authenticated loopback control
socket with private 0600 descriptors. CLI status displays the last persisted
checkpoint and distinguishes online from offline or recovery-required state. 

 The restart-budget checkpoint is a 0600 JSON file under the owner's private
 app-controls-<uid   directory. It stores retry timestamps  before  each
attempt. A supervisor restarted with the same configuration inherits the
remaining sliding-window budget, preventing hard crashes from resetting the
attempt limit. Configuration fingerprints intentionally reject changed commands,
ports, replica counts and restart windows unless the operator explicitly resets
the checkpoint with  fleet reset  while offline and fully recovered. 

   Operational limits:   This manages local processes, not distributed replicas.
The proxy must remain accessible via authenticated local control. Recovery
refuses live or unverifiable owners and cannot always discover orphaned process
grandchildren after their original leader disappears. Status is a last-known
snapshot if its writer encounters a disk error; the restart-budget persistence
hook fails closed rather than silently allowing a new replacement. A health
failure can temporarily reduce serving capacity. Full native Windows/macOS
integration and long-duration deployment tests are still required.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Dynamic fleet capacity and request-rate autoscaling (Section 28)
text:
A fleet can now change its desired replica count while running. Each new replica
is started and health-checked   before   its port is atomically added to the
route lease. Scale-down removes the selected port from new traffic first, waits
for in-flight HTTP and WebSocket connections (up to the configured drain
limit), then terminates the child. The fleet keeps at least one spare port.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Automatic capacity policy
text:
Autoscaling uses   requests per second per active healthy replica  , observed
by the  real proxy  rather than the fleet supervisor. The policy scales one
replica per decision, requires consecutive samples, uses different scale-up and
scale-down thresholds, and honors a cooldown. A manual  fleet scale  pauses
autoscaling until explicitly resumed. A failed or stale metrics request cannot
trigger a downscale; degraded fleets do not automatically downscale. 

 Only 2–16 replicas are supported, and the reserved port pool must contain
at least one extra port beyond the configured maximum. Scale operations are
serialized with health reconciliation. A partial scale-up error retains
healthy serving instances; reconciliation repairs missing desired capacity
within the durable replacement budget.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Persisted state and troubleshooting
text:
Fleet checkpoints retain desired replica count, restart attempt timestamps,
autoscaling pause state, and cooldown timestamp. Restart with the   same  
command, ports, baseline replica count, and scaling policy to restore state.
Configuration changes require deliberate checkpoint reset after verifying
all old generations are stopped. Private event history retains up to 100
lifecycle events for 30 days;  fleet doctor  reports offline owners, capacity
shortfalls, route mismatch and stale checkpoints without changing processes. 

   Operational caveats:   metrics are a bounded in-memory rolling window and
reset when the proxy restarts; they are not an observability database. A drain
limit can disconnect long-lived WebSockets. Scaling is local-process
orchestration, not cluster autoscaling; it does not provision machines, limit
CPU/memory usage, or distribute control across hosts. The OS and full app
integration still need validation in your deployment environment.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Fleet observability and resource autoscaling (Section 29)
text:
The fleet controller supports request-rate scaling (default) and Linux child-process
resource scaling. Samples are based on   the serving child processes  , not the
ZHOST controller process. Memory is the mean resident set size (RSS) in MiB per
replica; CPU usage is a percentage of   one CPU core   per replica (and may
exceed 100% for multithreaded work). 

 

 Existing request-rate flags ( --scale-up-rps ,  --scale-down-rps ) continue to
work. For resource modes, provide  --scale-up  and  --scale-down . On non-Linux
platforms, resource autoscaling fails at startup instead of emitting unsafe
zero-load observations. The first CPU sample warms up its counter baseline;
a replaced PID must also warm up before new readings can be trusted. 

   Scale-down safeguards:    --scale-max-error-rate  and  --scale-max-p95  require
recent, authenticated proxy telemetry. A response-error ratio or p95 latency
above the configured limit prevents a scale-down decision; malformed, missing,
or stale telemetry blocks sampling. WebSocket connection lifetimes are excluded
from HTTP latency measurements. Recent HTTP completion history is bounded per
backend, so p95 is an approximate percentile of the retained sample rather
than a full histogram. No server metrics endpoint is publicly exposed. 

 Metrics exports are read through the existing authenticated local CLI control.
The  --prometheus  format prints text to stdout for collection by an operator;
it does   not   enable an unauthenticated HTTP endpoint. Private autoscaling
observation history is retained for 24 hours, capped at 240 points, and written
no more frequently than every 30 seconds. State files remain owner-only and
symlinked or malformed files are rejected. A  fleet doctor --live  inspection
cross-checks real backend readiness, error rate and p95 latency; the original
offline  fleet doctor  continues to inspect durable state and ownership. 

 For production, always benchmark target workload, tune scale thresholds and
cooldowns, and test failures under sustained load. Linux  /proc  resource
monitoring is local-only, uses the operating system's conventional 100 Hz user
clock, and does not measure subprocess descendants or container-wide memory.
The metrics and scaling policy do not replace a distributed orchestrator,
container limits, autoscaler SLOs, or a monitoring time-series database.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Production consolidation: proxy, TLS, development server and resource limits
text:
The management proxy now   listens on  127.0.0.1  by default  , not every
network interface. This is important because registered development apps and
fleet controls are meant to be local. To deliberately expose the proxy on a
network, specify an address explicitly: 

 

 Only numeric IP addresses and  localhost  are accepted for  --bind . Binding
publicly is an operator decision: the proxy is not an Internet-facing ingress
controller with authentication, rate limiting, WAF, or tenant isolation. 

 When  --https  is selected, the proxy   rejects plaintext HTTP   on the TLS
port by default with HTTP 426. Library consumers that explicitly need the
legacy dual-protocol port can pass  allowPlainHttp: true  to
 createProxyServer . Certificates generated by the local CA no longer cause
an automatic machine-wide trust-store update. Use the   explicit  
 zerux-server trust  command after inspecting the CA and understanding its
implications. Dynamic TLS certificates are restricted to the configured local
TLD namespace and exact requested hostnames. Cached contexts and concurrent
certificate generation are bounded. 

 HTTP request and response headers now filter both fixed hop-by-hop headers
and the additional fields nominated by  Connection ; WebSocket handshakes
retain the necessary upgrade headers. Managed  /etc/hosts  entries are
validated and malformed managed blocks fail closed. 

 The dev-server implementation is now under  src/dev/ , with  src/index.ts 
remaining the package's public export surface. Dev HTML injection is limited
to 2 MiB of identity-encoded HTML; larger and compressed responses are
forwarded without injection rather than buffered unboundedly. The dev app
listens on loopback, filesystem watch reloads are serialized, and shutdown
releases its watcher without stopping unrelated applications' proxy. 

 For Linux fleets,  readLinuxContainerLimits()  reports cgroup v1/v2 CPU quota
and memory limit/usage where available. These container-wide figures are
  diagnostics  , not an invented per-child memory/CPU reading; missing and
unlimited constraints are represented as  null .
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Compatibility notes
text:
- A proxy intentionally accessed from another device now needs  --bind .
- Mixed HTTP and HTTPS on the same port now requires  allowPlainHttp: true .
- Trusting a new local certificate authority is now an explicit operation.
-  startServer  no longer stops a potentially shared proxy when its dev app exits.
- HTTP responses whose bodies are too large or encoded are no longer altered to inject the dev client.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Verification and limits
text:
The focused TypeScript check and regression tests exercise request filtering,
loopback binding validation, local certificates, hosts blocks, HTTPS downgrade
handling, dev HTML buffering, cgroup parsing, and the established routing,
WebSocket, and fleet APIs. A full monorepo install, native macOS/Windows test,
external exposure penetration test, and production load test are still required
before calling a deployment production-certified.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Optional proxy request limits
text:
Configure limits before binding; duplicate flags, partial numbers, and invalid
ranges are rejected: 

 

 Equivalent library options are available through  createProxyServer({limits}) .
 --rate  is a per-direct-IP sustained request rate,  --burst  is its token-bucket
capacity,  --max-active  is a global count of concurrent HTTP and upgraded
connections, and  --max-body  is a streamed request-body byte limit. Limits
are opt-in for compatibility. They are local process protections,   not  
a substitute for an authenticated public reverse proxy or distributed DDoS
protection. Size violations are rejected with HTTP 413, rate violations with
429, and concurrency overload with 503. Backend code may have seen a partial
chunked request before a streaming size violation is detected.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Integrated protocol gateway (Section 31)
text:
MCP has moved into  zhost   : import  createMcpServer ,  ToolRegistry ,
 ResourceRegistry  and  createProtocolGateway  from  zhost . The old
 @zeruxjs/mcp  package has been removed. MCP implements the stateless core
(tool/resource calls, initialize, ping) over Streamable HTTP JSON POST.
It is   not   a complete implementation of the MCP 2026-07-28 protocol
(subscriptions, elicitation, sampling, full metadata validation, etc.). 

 

 Protocol endpoints are  POST /mcp ,  POST /rpc ,
 POST /<package.Service /<Method   for   Connect unary JSON  ,  POST /trpc/<procedure  
for the basic tRPC-compatible procedure bridge, and  GET /events  for SSE.
The Connect and tRPC bridges are lightweight JSON subsets: use their official
framework adapters for full schema, codecs, bidirectional streams and client
compatibility. gRPC-over-HTTP/2 requests with  application/grpc  are forwarded
as streaming HTTP/2 to an h2c backend; other routes continue to use HTTP/1.1.
Keep these endpoints behind authentication if accessible outside a trusted local
machine. The gateway by default allows only loopback connections, validates
browser Origin, and caps request bodies. Supply  authorize(req)  for explicit
remote access control. Tool executions must also implement their own permission
checks before accessing sensitive data.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: HTTP versions and QUIC
text:
Version/transport   Support  
  ---   ---  
  HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1   Native Node HTTP server  
  HTTPS and HTTP/2   TLS ALPN negotiation, HTTP/1.1 fallback  
  HTTP/3 (QUIC)     External HTTP/3 terminator required  ; optional validated  Alt-Svc  advertising  
  WebTransport     External QUIC terminator required  ;  WebTransportRouter  lets a terminator attach real sessions  
  WebSocket   HTTP/1.1 upgrade proxy  
  SSE   Native streamed HTTP event source   

 Node 22's HTTP modules do not provide native HTTP/3 or WebTransport server APIs.
Do not configure  http3Terminator  unless a real QUIC listener is running at
that port with valid TLS certificates. For example: 

 

  http3Terminator  only publishes an  Alt-Svc  hint and capability metadata;
actual QUIC termination, HTTP/3 forwarding and WebTransport negotiation   must  
be provided by the external server. HTTP/2 ALPN happens automatically on the
native TLS server. Plain HTTP is not silently upgraded to TLS or QUIC. 

  proxy.getLoadStatus(windowMs?)  reports in-flight HTTP requests, request
arrival totals, protocol versions, response counts by status code and status
family (1xx–5xx), per-route latency and RPS, plus requests handled outside
registered application routes.  proxy.backendConnections.metrics()  continues
to provide backend-specific fleet telemetry. Aborted requests use a synthetic
 499  in the load API, not an HTTP status sent to the client. 

 Connect JSON streaming can be registered with
 protocols.connectStream.register('app.v1.Events', 'Watch', async function  (messages) { ... }) .
It uses Connect's five-byte framed  application/connect+json  responses,
including the end-stream envelope. Streaming is size bounded and does not
support compression or Protobuf encoding in this built-in lightweight adapter. 

 For application-specific load and Linux resource usage, call
 await proxy.getApplicationUsage('my-app.localhost', [workerPid]) . This returns
per-route HTTP response family counts, active upstream connections and optional
CPU/memory samples for   explicit   worker PIDs (first CPU sample is a warmup).
If you omit the PIDs, resource monitoring is not requested; unverified process
identities never produce fabricated zero-usage values.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Content compression (Brotli / gzip / deflate / Zstandard)
text:
ZHOST can compress eligible,   unencoded   HTTP responses while streaming the
body to the client. Negotiation observes  Accept-Encoding  quality weights,
explicit refusals, and  identity ;  Content-Encoding  and  Vary:
Accept-Encoding  describe the selected representation. Brotli, gzip and
deflate use built-in Node.js encoders;  zstd  is enabled only on runtimes with
native Zstandard support (experimental in Node 22.15+/23.8+). 

 

 Programmatically: 

 

   Reverse-proxy safety:   Existing upstream  Content-Encoding  is passed
through unchanged (not decompressed or compressed a second time). Nginx can
also compress responses at the outer boundary; it should respect the
pre-existing  Content-Encoding  and forward  Accept-Encoding  correctly. Use
 --no-compress  to make Nginx the sole compression layer. The proxy strips
invalidated body-specific headers ( Content-Length , strong ETags, digests,
range support) when compressing. It does not compress SSE, ranges/206, HEAD,
no-body statuses, or  Cache-Control: no-transform  responses. Upstream SSE
responses receive  X-Accel-Buffering: no  and  no-transform  to help protect
real-time delivery through Nginx. Already compressed but   unacceptable  
upstream representations return HTTP 406 instead of emitting content the
client cannot decode; configure upstreams to honor the original
 Accept-Encoding  for best compatibility. Unknown-length compressible streams
may still be compressed even if ultimately smaller than  minBytes . 

   Security:   Direct protocol gateway endpoints are private by default. If
Nginx or another front proxy forwards MCP/RPC to ZHOST, explicitly configure
 authorize(req) ; merely connecting from 127.0.0.1 is not a substitute for
user authentication. ZHOST denies forwarded requests without such an
allow-rule when recognized forwarding headers are present.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Forwarded-response compression
text:
HTTP responses can use streaming Brotli, gzip, deflate and Zstandard (where
Node exposes a Zstandard encoder), negotiated with  Accept-Encoding .
Configure  compression: { enabled: true, minBytes: 1024, brotliQuality: 4 } 
on  createProxyServer() , or set  compression: { enabled: false }  if your edge
server already compresses responses. The proxy avoids double-compression and
never transforms SSE, Connect/gRPC, range, or  Cache-Control: no-transform 
responses. Zstandard is only selected when the Node runtime supports it.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Proxy cache control (Section 32)
text:
Response caching is   off by default  , independent of ZHOST's streaming compression. To opt in: 

 

 Or set  createProxyServer({ getRoutes, proxyPort, cache: { enabled: true } }) . This exposes  proxy.responseCache.stats() ,  .invalidate(hostname, pathname?) , and  .clear()  for explicit invalidation. The proxy caches only HTTP 200 GET responses with explicit  Cache-Control: public, max-age=...  or  s-maxage , no cookies/authentication, no  Set-Cookie , no  Vary  or upstream  Content-Encoding , and no range, protocol stream or private/no-store response. Storage uses bounded process memory, not disk; entries expire and are separated by route generation. Cached identity bodies are compressed per client on delivery, so a gzip client and a Brotli client are never served the wrong encoding.  Age  reflects storage time. 

   Nginx deployment:   You can leave ZHOST compression disabled with  --no-compress  and use Nginx  gzip / brotli  instead. Already-compressed upstream responses always pass through unchanged. Do not configure both layers to compress the same response intentionally. SSE and Connect streams are neither buffered in ZHOST's cache nor compressed by ZHOST; configure Nginx  proxy_buffering off  for SSE as needed. Content-length, ETag, Vary and Accept-Encoding safety is handled by the proxy's compression layer; application-level cache policies remain authoritative.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: Reloading the development HTTP server
text: Development reloads now replace the active request handler without unbinding the application's HTTP port. In-flight requests retain their old handler, new requests use the new handler, and a failed  watchFunc  leaves the previous handler serving. This is local development lifecycle behavior, not a guarantee of zero-downtime production deployment.
description: Server Creator and Handle Auto load and so via @zerux/watcher

title: zlook
text:
zlook

Filesystem watcher for ZeruxJS, with   shared in-process subscriptions  , native notifications and a polling fallback. File updates are reported once after debouncing, and watchers are disposed when the last subscriber unsubscribes.

 

Events:  new ,  update ,  delete ; paths are relative to the watched root. Default exclusions:  .git ,  node_modules . Symbolic links are not traversed.  scan  and  diff  are exported for custom watcher integrations.

  Limitations:   sharing is process-local, not cross-process; polling uses file metadata, so a same-size write preserving modification time may be missed; a complete scan costs O(files). Filesystem read errors are surfaced through  onError . Watch paths should be trusted; callbacks execute in the caller's process.

    Shared watcher lifecycle

Use  watchDirectory()  when you need to await the baseline scan or force reconciliation:

 

Subscribers to the same directory share underlying watchers without sharing their ignore rules.  startWatcher()  is retained for existing callers and returns a disposal callback. The scanner does not traverse symlinks.

   Section 79 watcher validation

 watchDirectory(root, callback, { debounceMs, pollIntervalMs, onError }) 
validates callback/root types and integer millisecond settings before creating
any shared native watcher. Polling must be at least 100ms when configured;
intervals are bounded to ten minutes. Subscriber callbacks remain isolated,
errors are reported through  onError , and handles must be closed during hot
reload/unmount. Filesystem symlinks are never traversed by the recursive scan.
The fallback polling path is retained for hosts where recursive  fs.watch 
is unsupported. Test with  node --test test/ .test.mjs  after building.

   Release 0.0.2

Prepared to validate npm trusted publishing through GitHub Actions.

text:
Ztrial — test runner and assertion toolkit

Ztrial is a dependency-light test library for ZeruxJS, ZyroJS and ordinary JavaScript/TypeScript packages. It is   not   the ZyroJS UI runtime. The new API is modular, and existing  describe ,  test ,  expect  and  runTests  entry points remain available.

   Writing tests

 

Suite-scoped  beforeAll ,  afterAll ,  beforeEach , and  afterEach  hooks execute deterministically. Supports  test.only ,  test.skip ,  describe.only ,  describe.skip , timeout/retry limits, fail-fast  bail ,  forbidOnly , filtering, and callback result reporting.  createRunner()  creates an independent test registry that avoids cross-project global state.

Assertions include  toBe , circular-safe  toEqual ,  .not ,  toContain ,  toMatch ,  toHaveLength ,  toHaveProperty ,  toThrow ,  toReject  and  toResolve .  fn ,  spyOn , and  restoreAllMocks  supply lightweight spies.  waitFor  polls asynchronous conditions with an optional AbortSignal.

   CLI

Build first, then run  .test.js ,  .spec.js ,  .test.mjs , or  .spec.mjs  files:

 

Example JSON configuration:

 

The CLI has zero mandatory browser/test-runner dependencies. It imports runnable JavaScript test files; TypeScript test files must be transpiled or run through a separately configured TypeScript loader. JSON and TAP output are supported. Modules exported by  ztrial/jsdom  and  ztrial/playwright  are   optional adapters  ; the environment packages must be separately installed if those features are used. Vitest-shaped helpers do not replace Vitest's full mocking engine.

    Important limitations

Timeouts prevent the runner from waiting forever but cannot forcibly cancel an arbitrary test promise. Browser adapters require an installed browser/DOM environment; no native browser or Playwright automation is bundled. This is a focused foundation rather than a fully compatible replacement for Jest, Vitest, or Playwright.

   Verification

 

   Section 79 test-runner safeguards

-  --config  accepts a size-limited JSON file; a relative  root  in that file
  resolves from the file's directory, not the caller's working directory.
- CLI flags require values and numeric timeouts are bounded to ten minutes.
- Discovery ignores symlink entries,  .git ,  node_modules  and  dist .
- Zero matching files, zero registered test cases and  --match  selecting no
  runnable test cases now fail with exit code  2  instead of reporting a green run.
-  --bail  executes  afterAll  for suites already started; cleanup hook failures
  remain visible as test failures. Timeouts bound reporting but cannot forcibly
  cancel arbitrary JavaScript async operations.

Verify with  npm run build && node --test test/ .test.mjs . No browser/runtime
certification is inferred from source-only tests.

title: zuixs
text:
Zuixs

  Zuixs   (Zerux User Interface and Experience) is a utility-first, on-demand CSS compiler. It has no runtime framework dependency and is designed for   ZeruxJS  ,   ZyroJS  , React, Vue, Next.js, Nuxt and plain HTML.

   Getting started

 

In a consuming package, install  zuixs  and use the  zuix  binary. Add the generated stylesheet in the application's HTML root/layout. For dev regeneration, use  zuix watch -c zuix.config.mjs . The CLI scans  html ,  js ,  jsx ,  ts ,  tsx ,  vue ,  svelte ,  astro ,  md  and  mdx  by default and skips common build directories. Set  content  to constrain scanning on large projects.

 

 

   API

 

For a Vite-based app (including Vue, React, or Nuxt in Vite mode), use  zuixVite()  from  zuixs/vite , and import  virtual:zuix.css . The plugin is an early integration point; for reliable production builds with dynamically generated strings, prefer the CLI scanner and explicit  safelist  values.

   Utilities

Includes spacing, sizes, flex/grid/layout, typography, colors, palette shades, background, border, shadow, radii, positioning, overflow, display, responsive breakpoints, dark mode, pseudo states, group/peer states, arbitrary values ( w-[35px] ) and property utilities ( [scroll-margin-top:2rem] ). Variants can be chained, e.g.  md:dark:hover:bg-blue-700 . The  !  modifier marks declarations important. Responsive defaults:  sm  640px,  md  768px,  lg  1024px,  xl  1280px,  2xl  1536px.

 

  Limitations:   Static extraction recognizes literal class attributes and common class helpers, not all expressions or runtime-generated class names. Arbitrary values are accepted only from trusted application source code; don't compile raw classes submitted by untrusted users.  zuixVite  is intentionally framework-neutral and does not manage all bundler-specific invalidation cases yet. No changes to the ZeruxJS renderer or ZyroJS internals are required to use the generated CSS.

   Production improvements (0.2)

-   Idempotent output:   classes are deduplicated before generation; identical token inputs emit one rule. Configurable reset and plugin base CSS are emitted once per build.
-   Tree-shaken keyframes:   built-in  spin ,  pulse ,  bounce  and  ping  animation definitions are output only when their matching utilities are present; custom  keyframes  entries are supported.
-   Modern conditions:    cq-md: ,  container-[min-width:400px]: ,  supports-[display:grid]: ,  media-[width =700px]: ,  starting: ,  portrait: ,  landscape: ,  forced-colors: ,  contrast-more: ,  rtl: ,  ltr:  and  has-[.active]:  /  not-[.hidden]: .
-   Modern CSS utilities:   container sizing, scroll snap, overscroll, content-visibility, view transitions, color schemes, field sizing, text wrapping, subgrid, transition behaviors, filters, CSS scroll-driven animations, CSS anchor positioning and other properties via typed arbitrary utilities or  [property:value] .
